---
title: "Exercises — Pooled screens and synthetic libraries"
---

Pen and paper. Calculators are fine. These cover both decks: building a pooled library and
reading it out.

# Part 1 — Building the pool

## E1. Synthesis yield

An array vendor gives you 74-mers at 99.5% stepwise coupling, and offers 200-mers at the same
rate.

a. What fraction of the 74-mers and of the 200-mers are full length?
b. A pooled oligo carries a primer site at each end. Why do truncated products matter less
   than you might expect, and what do they still cost you?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
The yield is the coupling efficiency raised to the number of couplings, about n - 1.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 0.995^73 ≈ 0.69 and 0.995^199 ≈ 0.37. Over a third of a 200-mer pool is truncated.
b. A truncated molecule lacks one primer site and is not amplified by the primer pair, so it
   drops out at the PCR step. Errors *inside* the sequence (substitutions, deletions) stay in
   the pool and are cloned, and they show up as reads that match no design. Both reduce
   how much of the pool is usable.
:::

## E2. How many colonies

A 70,000-guide library is transformed into bacteria. Assume an even pool and Poisson sampling.

a. If you collect 5 colonies per guide on average, how many guides are expected to be missing?
b. And at 20 per guide?
c. Why is the real number higher than your estimate?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. e^-5 ≈ 0.67%, so about 470 guides.
b. e^-20 ≈ 2 x 10^-9: none.
c. The pool is not even (synthesis, PCR and clone growth all add skew), so some members start
   at a fraction of the mean. The Poisson estimate is a floor.
:::

## E3. Gibson or Golden Gate

You need (i) one guide in lentiCRISPR v2 for a validation experiment, and (ii) 70,000 guides
as a pool in the same vector. Which cloning method do you use for each, and which property of
the method decides?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
(i) Annealed oligos with CACC and AAAC overhangs into a BsmBI-cut vector: the overhangs fix
orientation and the construct is easy to verify. (ii) Gibson assembly of the amplified pool: it
needs only homology at the ends, which the shared constant parts of the pool provide, and it
joins every member in one reaction without designing 70,000 overhangs. The deciding property
is whether the design must be per member or the same for all of them.
:::

# Part 2 — Delivering it

## E4. One copy per cell

a. At a multiplicity of 0.2, what fraction of cells receive 0, 1, or 2 or more copies?
b. Of the infected cells, what fraction has two or more?
c. You want at most about 10% of infected cells to carry two guides. Is 0.2 acceptable?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. P(0) = e^-0.2 = 0.819; P(1) = 0.2 x 0.819 = 0.164; P(2+) = 1 - 0.819 - 0.164 = 0.018.
b. 0.018 / (1 - 0.819) ≈ 10%.
c. Just acceptable. Going lower reduces doubles but wastes more cells.
:::

## E5. Cell numbers

A 70,000-guide library, 300 cells per guide, MOI 0.2 (18% of cells infected).

a. How many cells must be infected?
b. After selection you harvest 21 million cells. How much DNA is that, at 6.6 pg per cell?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Cells carrying a guide: 70,000 x 300 = 21 million. Infected cells needed: 21 million /
   0.18 ≈ 117 million.
b. 21 x 10^6 x 6.6 pg ≈ 139 µg of DNA, which is why a whole screen sample needs many PCR
   reactions.
:::

## E6. The swapped barcode

Two vector designs: (A) the guide is in U6 and a 12-nt barcode is placed in a separate
transcript 2 kb away; (B) the guide itself is the readout. Pooled lentivirus is made from a
plasmid pool.

a. In which design can the link between guide and readout be broken, and by what?
b. How does this change when you read guides directly from genomic DNA?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. In (A). A particle contains two RNA copies; reverse transcriptase can jump from one to
   the other, so a barcode can end up beside a different guide. The further apart the two
   elements, the likelier this is. In (B) there is nothing to separate.
b. Reading guides from genomic DNA does not depend on a barcode, so this swap cannot occur.
:::

# Part 3 — Reading out

## E7. Reactions per sample

Each 50 µL PCR takes 3.5 µg of gDNA. How many reactions are needed for 100 µg per sample, and
for 40 samples? What does that tell you about where the protocol should put its indexes?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
100 / 3.5 ≈ 29 reactions per sample, so about 1,150 for 40 samples. That many reactions with
long indexed primers is expensive and a contamination risk. A two-step design uses short
locus-specific primers for the many first reactions, pools them, and indexes only one small
second reaction per sample.
:::

## E8. Depth per sample after pooling

The forty indexed libraries of a 70,000-guide screen are cut from a gel, quantified and pooled
for one run that returns 400 million reads. One library is quantified badly and goes in at half
the molarity of the other thirty-nine.

a. How many reads does each correctly pooled library get, and how many does the odd one get?
b. Express both as reads per guide.
c. About 100 reads per guide are needed to tell a twofold drop from counting noise. Which
   samples still qualify, and what does the gel cut before pooling have to do with that number?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Reads follow molarity. Count the pool in units of one full-strength library.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. The pool is 39 + 0.5 = 39.5 units, so a unit gets 400 / 39.5 ≈ 10.1 million reads. The
   thirty-nine get about 10.1 million each, the under-pooled one about 5.1 million.
b. 10.1 x 10^6 / 70,000 ≈ 145 reads per guide, and ≈ 72 for the odd sample.
c. The thirty-nine clear 100 reads per guide; the under-pooled sample does not, and its counts
   are the noisiest in the screen even though nothing went wrong in its PCRs. Primer dimers
   cluster, so any that survived into the pool would take reads out of the same 400 million,
   and they also inflate a fluorescence-based quantification, which is how a library ends up at
   the wrong molarity in the first place.
:::

## E9. A low-diversity library

You run a single-primer-type amplicon library with a 2% PhiX spike-in, and the run fails in
the first cycles.

a. Why?
b. How do the Joung and Moffat protocols each handle this?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Every molecule begins with the same sequence, so each cluster shows the same base in the
   first cycles and the instrument cannot calibrate cluster positions and colours.
b. Joung: ten forward primers with spacers of different length, so the start differs between
   amplicons. The Moffat protocol skips the constant part with dark cycles and relies on the
   run design for diversity.
:::

## E10. Where a count came from

A two-step readout runs 25 cycles in the first PCR and 10 in the second. Three guides come back
odd. Guide A has fifty times the median count, in one sample only. Guide B is low in every
sample of the screen, and was also low in the plasmid pool that was sequenced before the
experiment. Guide C is low in every sample, sat at the median in the plasmid pool, and is 78% GC.

a. For each guide, say where the number came from.
b. Splitting the 100 µg over 29 first-round reactions is forced by how much DNA one reaction
   takes, but it also defends against one of these three. Which, and how?
c. For a count to be of molecules rather than of copies, what must be true of the tag that
   carries the count, and at which step of this protocol would it have to be attached?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Thirty-five cycles separate the tube from the counts. Two of the three oddities appear in every
sample, one in a single tube; one of them is older than the screen itself.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. A is jackpotting: a template copied in an early cycle of the first PCR keeps that lead
   through all 35 cycles and returns as one enormous count. It is one tube's accident, so it is
   in one sample. B was already skewed in the plasmid pool, so it is no PCR effect at all and no
   screen result either; that is what sequencing the pool first is for. C is sequence-dependent
   amplification efficiency: a high-GC amplicon is copied less well in both PCRs, in every
   sample alike.
b. A. Each of the 29 reactions amplifies its own share of the genomic DNA, so an early lead in
   one of them is diluted by the other 28 products when they are pooled. A real enrichment is
   present in all 29.
c. The tag must be attached once per starting molecule, before anything is amplified. A tag in
   either PCR primer is drawn afresh in every cycle and so labels copies — the rule is in the
   barcodes-and-UMIs unit. In a genomic readout that means the tag arrives on a probe or an
   adapter that touches each molecule a single time, which is the molecular-inversion-probe
   route built and traced in the targeted-sequencing unit.
:::

## E11. Pick the anchor

A lentiviral library integrated into human cells; you want the integration sites of 20 clones.
You know the LTR sequence only.

a. Describe inverse PCR for this problem: what must be true of the restriction enzyme?
b. What goes wrong if the ligation is concentrated?
c. What does a splinkerette adapter add?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Inverse PCR and the splinkerette are taught as blocks in the amplification unit, and the blocked
hairpin that makes a one-sided ligation stay one-sided in the end-chemistry unit. What is asked
here is what the lentiviral case demands of each.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. The enzyme should cut in the flank and once on the known side, so that each junction
   fragment has the known part at one end, the unknown flank at the other, and both primer
   sites between. Enzymes that cut often give fragments too short to map.
b. Fragments ligate to each other and form concatemers and hybrid circles, giving chimeric
   products. Dilute ligation favours intramolecular circles.
c. A second primer site that exists only on molecules copied from the known side. Genomic
   ends that carry only adapter cannot prime, which cuts the background.
:::

## E12. Activity from tags

In an MPRA, tag A has 100 DNA and 400 RNA counts, tag B has 40 DNA and 160 RNA, and tag C has
100 DNA and 100 RNA. Which candidates are active? What would you conclude if you looked at RNA
counts alone?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
RNA/DNA is 4 for A and B and 1 for C: A and B are equally active, C is not. The RNA counts
alone would suggest A is far more active than B (400 against 160), but A simply had more
plasmids in the DNA pool. Normalising to DNA removes that difference.
:::

## E13. Design a display readout

A colleague has panned a phage library of randomised 16-amino-acid peptides against an
immobilised human receptor. They have done four rounds, picked 40 colonies and Sanger-sequenced
them. Three sequences appear repeatedly, and they are ready to call those the hits.

a. Give two reasons the three repeated sequences might not be the best binders.
b. Design a sequencing readout of the round-by-round pools instead. Say what you amplify,
   where the primer sites come from, and what quantity you compare between rounds.
c. They also want to know how many *molecules* of each variant were present, not just the
   read fraction. What do you add, and at which step must it be added?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Ask what four rounds of binding, washing and amplification select for besides affinity. For
(c), remember the rule from the barcodes-and-UMIs unit about where a UMI can and cannot be
introduced.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Repetition measures *amplification*, not affinity. A peptide that grows faster in the
   host, or that binds the plastic, the streptavidin or the blocking protein rather than the
   receptor, is enriched by exactly the same cycle. Forty colonies also sample only the very
   top of a pool that may still hold millions of variants, so nothing is learnt about the
   distribution.
b. The variable 48 nt sit between two constant flanks in the phage genome, so the readout is
   an ordinary amplicon: amplify the variable region with primers in those flanks, carrying
   the sequencing handles as tails, in two steps so the index is added last. Sequence the
   input pool and every round. The quantity to compare is each variant's *enrichment ratio*
   between consecutive rounds, not its abundance in the final round — that separates real
   binders from things that were already common.
c. A UMI on the first-round primer, that is, introduced in the single extension that first
   copies each template, before any exponential amplification. A UMI added in a later PCR
   cycle tags copies rather than original molecules and so counts nothing useful.
:::

# Self-check

1. Why does an oligo pool contain constant ends?
2. What is the purpose of sequencing the plasmid pool?
3. Name two things that make the number of cells decide how many guides you can keep.
4. Why does a one-end-known problem need a trick?
5. What do UMIs correct that read counts do not?
6. In display, what holds a protein variant and its own gene together?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. One primer pair amplifies every member, and the ends give homology for cloning.
2. It is the time-zero reference and the check of completeness, evenness and correctness.
3. Coverage per guide times library size sets the minimum cells; the multiplicity of infection
   sets how many must be infected.
4. PCR needs two primer sites; the unknown side has none until it is circularised, ligated to
   an adapter or tagged.
5. PCR duplication: they count original molecules, not copies.
6. The particle or complex itself: the phage carries its DNA inside and the variant on its
   coat; ribosome display keeps the mRNA, ribosome and protein as one complex; mRNA and click
   display use a covalent linker. No cell is involved.
:::
